evidence: "1. Workload metrics — what the system is being asked to do. Requests per second (rps) and the token profile (input length, output length, context length). These are the independent variables — the offered load; we do not control them, we characterize them. Admitted concurrency is a serving/scheduler state (Little's law), not a workload input. Fig 6.1's workload box lists concurrency alongside rps and the token profile: read that entry as offered concurrency — the arrival-side λ that the traffic offers — not as admitted or queued concurrency, which sits on the serving/scheduler side with queue depth."
issue: Figure/body ontology contradiction (recurrence family: figure-vs-body classification conflicts). The body text now declares that Fig 6.1's workload box 'lists concurrency alongside rps and the token profile' and instructs the reader to reinterpret it as offered/arrival-side concurrency. The figure itself (rendered p. 129) shows the box labelled literally 'Workload metrics / rps · token profile · concurrency'. A figure that says 'concurrency' in a workload box, paired with a body sentence that must instruct the reader how NOT to read that box's own label, is a labelling defect: the figure's text contradicts the classification the prose admits it needs. The caption on p. 129 repeats the repair instruction ('Label caveat: the workload box's concurrency entry is offered concurrency (arrival-side), not admitted or queued concurrency') rather than fixing the figure, which means the taxonomy in the artifact is wrong and the prose is carrying an erratum. Same defect family as the queue-depth entry, which the figure places in a separate dashed band labelled 'scheduler state, not a serving metric' — concurrency receives no such treatment in the figure, only in prose.
fix_instruction: Edit Fig 6.1 so the workload box reads 'rps · token profile · offered concurrency (λ)' (or move concurrency into a distinct arrival-side band parallel to the queue-depth band), so the figure's own text is not contradicted by the caption's caveat. Alternatively relabel the box to 'offered load: rps · token profile' and drop 'concurrency' from the figure entirely, keeping the arrival-side concurrency notion only in the body text. Then shorten the caption's 'Label caveat' sentence to a pointer rather than an erratum.

evidence: Figure 6.1 in-figure text: 'Workload metrics / rps · token profile · concurrency', 'Resource metrics / HBM BW · MFU · KV occupancy · memory pressure', 'Serving metrics / TTFT · TPOT · goodput', and a separate band 'queue depth: scheduler state, not a serving metric'.
issue: List-of-Figures / in-figure-heading divergence. The List of Figures (p. 10) describes Fig 6.1 as 'The metric hierarchy as a diagnostic chain [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]'. The in-figure headings, however, are not neutral labels: the workload box says 'concurrency', while the body's §6.1.1 and the caption both insist concurrency is a serving/scheduler state and not a workload input. The figure therefore promotes a taxonomy error into an artifact that readers consult as a quick reference. This is a second, independent occurrence of the same defect family in a different form (the first being the caption's repair instruction), and it will recur wherever a figure in this book is used as a standalone reference card.
fix_instruction: Regenerate Fig 6.1 with the three box headings matching the taxonomy exactly: 'Workload: rps · token profile · offered concurrency (λ)', 'Serving: TTFT · TPOT · goodput', 'Resource: HBM BW · MFU · KV occupancy · memory pressure', and keep queue depth in the scheduler-state band with an explicit 'scheduler state' label. Then verify the List of Figures entry (p. 10) still describes the figure accurately and that no other figure reuses the un-qualified term 'concurrency' in a workload box.

evidence: "Evidence boundary — four registers, and where each is used. MEASURED — an instrumented run under the Chapter 14 protocol; used only where the book reports a benchmark it actually ran, never for a planning screen. ANALYTICAL — arithmetic on stated inputs (roofline, KV-residency and capacity screens, the C/W per-host bound and the host counts derived from it): a bound, not an observed rate — not a measured throughput, not a lower guaranteed rate, not SLO-goodput, no p95/p99 guarantee, each conditional on its stated assumptions (e.g. the assumed mean KV residency time). ILLUSTRATIVE — a chosen scenario input or worked example ([canonical scenario] or [ILLUSTRATIVE], paired with ASSUMPTION or DERIVED), on the book's teaching geometry, to be re-derived per deployment; this is a provenance-and-register marker, not a measurement status (see the Axis note below). HYPOTHESIS — reasoned but not yet validated (with UNRESOLVED for questions the book leaves open), used where mechanism is argued without measurement."
issue: Self-contradictory label definitions in the Preface, the document's own rule source. The Preface simultaneously asserts (a) four measurement registers, MEASURED / ANALYTICAL / ILLUSTRATIVE / HYPOTHESIS, each with a stated use; and (b) a three-axis label-pair system in which ILLUSTRATIVE is explicitly reclassified: 'this is a provenance-and-register marker, not a measurement status'. The second clause cancels the fourth register: if ILLUSTRATIVE is a provenance tag and never a measurement status, it cannot simultaneously be one of the four measurement registers. The paragraph then lists ANALYTICAL, SCENARIO-DERIVED, MODELED, MEASURED as the measurement-status vocabulary — five names, of which ANALYTICAL is drawn from the 'four registers' list and three are not in it at all. A reader cannot determine, from the Preface alone, which of the two taxonomies governs a given tag, and the two are used interchangeably throughout the body (e.g. p. 149 '[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]' on Fig 7.7 versus p. 169's '[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]'; and p. 20's 'Forward-looking numbers are marked ILLUSTRATIVE', i.e. ILLUSTRATIVE as a measurement status).
fix_instruction: Rewrite the Preface 'Evidence boundary' panel so there is exactly one taxonomy: a two-axis label-pair system (Axis 1 provenance ∈ {1P, canonical scenario, ILLUSTRATIVE, 2°, LAB} × Axis 2 epistemic ∈ {FACT, DERIVED, ASSUMPTION, HYPOTHESIS, UNRESOLVED}) plus a separate Axis 3 measurement-status vocabulary (ANALYTICAL / SCENARIO-DERIVED / MODELED / MEASURED / UNMEASURED). Delete the 'four registers' framing, or explicitly subordinate it ('the four registers below are shorthand for the most common (Axis 2, Axis 3) combinations; the label pair is authoritative'). Then sweep the body for any use of ILLUSTRATIVE or HYPOTHESIS as a standalone measurement status and re-tag those rows.

evidence: "A label pair always takes one item from each of the first two axes, e.g. [1P][DERIVED] or [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]; the two tags are set with no space between them and never break across a line." Compare p. 17: "Every load-bearing quantitative claim carries Axes 1 and 2 as an inline pair (e.g. [1P][DERIVED])" and "Axis 3, measurement status, rides along where a claim's status is known."
issue: Illegal/undocumented label pair forms in the body that the Preface's rule does not authorise, and no statement of what a three-tag sequence means. The Preface states a label pair takes one item from each of the first two axes, with Axis 3 riding along. The body nonetheless uses multi-tag sequences that combine an Axis-2 epistemic tag with a third tag in a way the Preface never defines, including p. 19 '[1P][DERIVED] (Wan2.2 sampling loop, pinned revision 1ea34ff, retrieved 2026-10-28.)' and p. 135 '[DERIVED] (source keys: each [S#] names one entry in the References chapter...)' — where the bracketed Axis-2 tag is followed by a source key rather than an Axis-3 status. Worse, p. 135 reads: '"[1P][DERIVED] [HYPOTHESIS]"' — no; the actual text is 'These percentages are hypothetical telemetry signatures ... [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]' while the sentence two lines earlier reads 'a decode kernel pinned at ~95% of HBM bandwidth / ~30% of FLOPs [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]'. The genuine double-pair violation appears at p. 135 in the sentence '[S4][1P][FACT]: the bottleneck-regime difference is the primary motivation for disaggregation' where an Axis-3-style 'MEASURED' claim rides with [1P][FACT], and at p. 139 'DFlash reports over 6× lossless acceleration ... [S5][1P][FACT] — because it reduces weight reads per accepted token' where a paper-reported figure is tagged [1P][FACT] although the Preface reserves [1P] for 'the model vendor's own spec'.
fix_instruction: Either (a) extend the Preface to define the permitted multi-tag sequences (e.g. '[1P][FACT] + MEASURED' and '[S#] [1P][FACT] + SCENARIO-DERIVED') and state that a source key '[S#]' is not an axis tag; or (b) normalise every occurrence so that exactly one Axis-1 tag and one Axis-2 tag appear, with the Axis-3 status either omitted or set in a declared form. Specifically re-check p. 135 ('[S4][1P][FACT]'), p. 138 ('[S5][1P][FACT]'), p. 139 ('[S7][1P][FACT]') and p. 19 ('[1P][FACT] (Wan2.2 sampling loop...)') so the tag set matches the Preface's declared grammar.

evidence: "[DERIVED] (source keys: each [S#] names one entry in the References chapter, where [S3]–[S7] resolve; Ch 11 lists [S1]–[S6] inline.)"
issue: Malformed / self-contradictory source-key pointer. The sentence states that '[S3]–[S7] resolve' and then immediately states 'Ch 11 lists [S1]–[S6] inline' — the two ranges overlap only partially ([S3]–[S6]) and the [S#] keyspace is not reconciled: if Ch 11 lists S1–S6 and Ch 6 uses S3–S7, then S7 appears in Ch 6 while the Ch 11 inline range stops at S6, leaving S7 without a stated home until the References chapter. The pointer form is also non-declared: the Preface's cross-reference conventions (p. 20) declare only '§ N.M', 'Ch N §M' and appendix 'A.N' forms; '[S#]' is an undocumented reference form. This is part of the malformed-cross-reference family: an undocumented pointer syntax used repeatedly across Chs 6, 11 and the References chapter.
fix_instruction: Add '[S#]' to the Preface's declared cross-reference forms with the rule for its resolution (one entry in the References chapter), and reconcile the ranges: state explicitly which keys each chapter uses and which are shared (e.g. 'S1–S7 are book-wide; Ch 11 discusses S1–S6; S7 is introduced in Ch 6'). Fix the sentence so it no longer asserts two overlapping ranges without reconciliation.

evidence: "Speculative decoding where decode bandwidth is the wall — DFlash reports over 6× lossless acceleration, up to 2.5× over EAGLE-3, in its paper's evaluated configurations [S5][1P][FACT] — because it reduces weight reads per accepted token. These are paper-reported results, not portable serving-speed figures: treat them as performance claims to re-measure on the target workload, not as a guaranteed speedup."
issue: Label/provenance mismatch: the Preface (p. 17) defines [1P] as 'first-party: the model vendor's own spec', and the evidence boundary on p. 5 scopes [1P] to 'the model vendor's own spec'. A third-party research paper's own self-reported speedup is first-party relative to the paper but is not a 'model vendor's own spec' of the deployed model. The sentence itself concedes these are 'paper-reported results, not portable serving-speed figures' — i.e. the measurement status is PAPER-REPORTED / UNVALIDATED, not MEASURED, yet the tag pair given is [1P][FACT]. Same pattern at p. 135 ('Mooncake: a 525% throughput increase (simulated) and 75% more requests [S4][1P][FACT]') and p. 139 ('vLLM KV-offloading ... cuts TTFT by 2–22× in a particular warm-cache-hit/reuse benchmark ... [S7][1P][FACT]'), where a 'simulated' figure carries a [FACT] tag.
fix_instruction: Add a provenance tag for 'first-party to a third-party research paper, as reported by its authors' (e.g. [PAPER]) or state in the Preface that [1P] means 'first-party to the cited source (vendor spec or paper's own reported result)' and extend Axis 3 with a status for 'as-reported-by-source, not independently reproduced'. Then re-tag the DFlash, Mooncake and vLLM-KV-offload figures accordingly, keeping the 'simulated' qualifier visible in the tag rather than only in prose.

evidence: "Scenario A [ILLUSTRATIVE]: the extra 20 tok/s are produced, but they land in the tail that misses the SLO, so goodput does not grow. Raw throughput is up 40%; goodput (tokens that met the SLO) is effectively unchanged in this case, because the batch of SLO-compliant tokens didn't grow." — followed by "Scenario B [ILLUSTRATIVE]: if the compliant fraction falls from 96% to 94%, goodput is 50×0.96 = 48 vs 70×0.94 = 65.8 — it rises despite the p95 breach." and "Scenario C [ILLUSTRATIVE]: if the compliant fraction falls to 65% ... goodput is 70×0.65 = 45.5 tok/s — below the 48 tok/s baseline."
issue: Illegal/ambiguous evidence label: an epistemic-status tag has been attached to a scenario label rather than to a claim. The Preface (p. 18) defines the Axis-2 vocabulary as 'FACT — directly stated by the source; DERIVED — computed by arithmetic from stated inputs; ASSUMPTION — a deliberately chosen scenario input, paired with a scenario provenance ([canonical scenario] or [ILLUSTRATIVE]); HYPOTHESIS — reasoned but not yet validated; UNRESOLVED'. 'Scenario A/B/C' is a scenario identifier, and '[ILLUSTRATIVE]' is an Axis-1 provenance tag; attaching it to a scenario name ('Scenario A [ILLUSTRATIVE]') rather than to the proposition makes the pair ambiguous — there is no Axis-2 element, so the 'label pair' rule on p. 18 ('a label pair always takes one item from each of the first two axes') is violated three times in one paragraph block. The body then does supply the arithmetic (f ≈ 68.6%), but the Scenario A statement is asserted ('goodput does not grow') without a tag stating it is a DERIVED conclusion — and in fact Scenario A is only true if f = 68.6%, which the text says itself.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the three scenarios so each carries a proper pair, e.g. 'Scenario A [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: at f = 68.6% (48 ÷ 70), goodput is unchanged at 48 tok/s', 'Scenario B [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: at f = 94%, goodput = 65.8 tok/s', 'Scenario C [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: at f = 65%, goodput = 45.5 tok/s'. Remove the bare '[ILLUSTRATIVE]' after the scenario names and add the missing 'DERIVED' that the arithmetic in the text performs.

evidence: "Forward-looking numbers are marked ILLUSTRATIVE."
issue: Evidence-label taxonomy violation in the Preface's own conventions: ILLUSTRATIVE is used here as a standalone marker on a class of numbers (a measurement/validity status), which the Preface's Axis note on p. 17 explicitly forbids — '"[ILLUSTRATIVE] is a provenance tag (Axis 1) only — a non-canonical worked example — and is never a measurement status'. 'Forward-looking' is a validity/provenance-of-knowledge statement, not a provenance-of-source statement, so the tag cannot express it. There is no tag in the declared vocabulary for 'projected / forward-looking' — [HYPOTHESIS] is the closest but is not used here. This is the same defect family as EV-001 (register taxonomy vs label pairs), in the conventions section rather than the evidence panel.
fix_instruction: Replace with a defined tag, e.g. 'Forward-looking numbers are marked [HYPOTHESIS] (Axis 2) and, where they are worked examples on the canonical geometry, also [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]' — and add the forward-looking notion to the Preface's Axis-2 definition so the convention is defined rather than improvised.

evidence: "2. What fits on one host? — weight residency, KV per token, the concurrency floor. (Chs. 3, 7)" ... "5. Who serves it, and how? — batching, parallelism, P/D disaggregation, scheduling. (Chs. 10–11, 20)" ... "Q1 in Part II, Q2–3 in Parts I/III, Q4–5 in Parts III–V, Q6 in Parts IV/VI."
issue: Malformed cross-reference form: the Preface (p. 20) declares the section-reference grammar 'A section reference takes the form § N.M, which means Chapter N, Section M — so § 1.4 is Ch. 1, Section 4 (Measurement), not Section 1's fourth subsection.' and adds 'Do not repeat a chapter number after the chapter name — write Ch. 8 § 3 or § 8.3.3, not Ch. 8 § 8.3.3.' The checklist's parentheticals use a bare multi-chapter form '(Chs. 3, 7)' and '(Chs. 10–11, 20)' with no section anchors at all, so the reader cannot tell which of the many sections in Ch 7 or Ch 11 is meant — this is exactly the 'bare §7' family the blind-spot note flags, in a different notation. The 'Q1…Q6' shorthand is also an undocumented reference form: 'Q2–3' is not a section, a chapter or a figure, and no list of 'Q' targets exists anywhere in the book.
fix_instruction: Give each checklist item section-level anchors in the declared § N.M form (e.g. '§ 7.3 and § 7.6', '§ 10.1–§ 11.4, § 20.2'), and either define the Q1–Q6 shorthand explicitly in the Preface (as an index into the six checklist items) or replace it with the same section anchors. Then sweep the book for other bare '(Chs. X, Y)' pointers and add anchors.

evidence: "Cross-references. A section reference takes the form § N.M, which means Chapter N, Section M — so § 1.4 is Ch. 1, Section 4 (Measurement), not Section 1's fourth subsection. Where the chapter is named first, the section number may stand alone: Ch. 7 § 3 means Ch. 7, Section 3."
issue: Ambiguous cross-reference rule as written: 'the section number may stand alone' does not specify whether the standalone form is '§ 3' or '§ 7.3', and the example given ('Ch. 7 § 3') uses a bare section number with no chapter digit, which is precisely the malformed '§7' form that the Preface then says it wants to avoid. The rule therefore authorises two incompatible notations and cannot be applied deterministically: '§ 7.3' is Chapter 7 Section 3 under the declared form, but '§ 3' after 'Ch. 7' means the same thing — so the same string '§ 3' means Ch 3 Section 3 in one context and Ch 7 Section 3 in another. The rule needs an explicit disambiguation rule (e.g. 'a standalone section number is always read against the most recently named chapter') plus a statement of what a bare '§ 7' without a chapter context means.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the rule: '§ N.M always means Chapter N, Section M. When a chapter is already named, write § M and read it against that chapter — but never write a bare § N where N could be mistaken for a chapter number: use § N.M in all other contexts.' Then audit the body for the bare '§ N' form and convert to § N.M.

evidence: "In the book's convention (Ch. 2, 4), TTFTe2e = retrieval + admission/queue + tokenization/transfer + prefill, where tokenization/transfer counts as one combined term." Compare p. 36 (Ch 2): "Written as a sum, end-to-end TTFT is TTFTe2e = retrieval + admission/queue + tokenization/transfer + prefill."
issue: Preface-vs-Ch.2 formula divergence in the reference form, and an unresolvable pointer. The Preface and Ch. 2 state the identical formula, but the Preface cites it as '(Ch. 2, 4)' — the declared § N.M convention is not used, and more importantly the pointer 'Ch. 2, 4' is ambiguous: does it mean Ch. 2 and Ch. 4 (both chapters), or Ch. 2 Section 4? Under the Preface's own rule that '§ 1.4 is Ch. 1, Section 4', the string 'Ch. 2, 4' has no defined interpretation. The same pattern recurs at p. 36: 'Ch 4 §4.3 quotes this formula verbatim' (a mixed 'Ch N §M.M' form that the Preface's 'write Ch. 8 § 3 or § 8.3.3, not Ch. 8 § 8.3.3' rule permits only in the first variant, but here the decimal is doubled in a way that collides with the § N.M grammar), and at p. 20: 'The book’s convention (Ch. 2, 4)'.
fix_instruction: Normalise every instance: use '§ 2.1 and § 4.3' rather than '(Ch. 2, 4)', and replace 'Ch 4 §4.3' with '§ 4.3'. Sweep the full document for the 'Ch N §N.M' doubled-decimal form and for comma-separated chapter lists without section anchors.

chapter: Ch 4 — The Anatomy of an AI Workload
evidence: "For this chapter, measurement is about quantifying the six dimensions so the workload can be communicated definitively and used to drive architecture decisions. The token-counting habits of § 1.4 apply unchanged (run the model’s own tokenizer, split input from output, log the distribution not just the mean) — rather than restate them, the three things the six-dimension view adds are:" ... and "These habits answer the book’s recurring question, 'what would I actually measure here?' — and they let the six dimensions be stated as numbers an architecture decision can be defended on."
issue: Bare malformed cross-reference: '§ 1.4' is written here without the 'Ch. 1' qualifier in a context where the declared § N.M grammar does apply (the section number is a decimal, so §1.4 does resolve to Ch 1 Section 4 — the form itself is legal). The defect is instead in the referenced target: the Preface (p. 20) states '§ 1.4 is Ch. 1, Section 4 (Measurement)', but Ch. 1's §1.4 heading is 'Measurement' and contains exactly three items ('Actual token count, not the rule of thumb', 'Input vs output split', 'Peak vs average context') — so the target does resolve correctly. However the same chapter uses the bare '§ 1.4' in at least one other place and the bare-chapter form '§ 7.3' etc. elsewhere; the recurring defect in this family is the mix of 'Ch 1 §1.4', '§ 1.4' and '§ 1.4's' with no declared disambiguation, and the Preface's own example sentence on p. 20 quotes § 1.4 as '(Measurement)' while the book's actual §1.4 heading on p. 32 is '1.4. Measurement' — consistent. This entry is therefore a weaker case; filed at P3 only for the unresolved 'Ch 2, 4'-style bare chapter pointer appearing in the same paragraph family.
fix_instruction: Where a bare '§ N.M' is used, ensure at least one chapter anchor appears in the same paragraph or the previous paragraph, and adopt a house rule that cross-references never rely on the reader remembering the current chapter. Apply to '§ 1.4' on this page and '§ 1.5' referenced as 'the tokenizer-side traps ... are § 1.5's'.

chapter: Ch 4 — The Anatomy of an AI Workload
evidence: "As Chapters 8 and 16–17 show, a single 8×H100 host holds ~17.5 KV-resident requests (436 GB KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per 9.5K-token resident request ≈ 17.51, §4.6). Whole-slot convention (canonical statement in § 7.3, Fig 7.7): the canonical concurrency ceiling is that resident-basis quotient floored to a whole slot — 17, not 18."
issue: Cross-reference that resolves to the wrong level of target, and a figure reference whose subject is misdescribed. '§4.6' is a bare § N.M pointing to Ch. 4 Section 6, which does exist (p. 105, 'Architecture Consequence') and does carry the 436 ÷ 24.9 ≈ 17.5 figure — so that pointer resolves. But '§ 7.3, Fig 7.7' pairs a section pointer with a figure pointer where Fig 7.7's caption and body (p. 149) state the byte-accurate value as 17.51 and the floor as 17, while the *figure's own in-figure text* reads '≈ 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB ≈ 17.5 → ~17 requests' and the caption's naming note says 'the arithmetic panel reads "in-flight"; that quantity is the KV-resident slot count (concurrent sequences holding a KV slot), not the Little's-Law in-flight request count'. The text here (and p. 105) uses 'KV-resident requests' — the figure's label ('in-flight') is the term the caption disowns, so a reader following the pointer lands on a figure whose own label contradicts the pointed-to quantity. This is the figure-vs-caption ontology defect in the concurrency family.
fix_instruction: Change the in-figure panel label in Fig 7.7 from 'in-flight ≈ KV budget ÷ KV per request' to 'KV-resident slots ≈ KV budget ÷ KV per request', so the figure's text matches the caption's own naming note and the §4.6/§7.3 terminology ('KV-resident requests', 'resident slots'). Then confirm the List of Figures entry for Fig 7.7 (p. 10, 'The concurrency budget') still matches.

chapter: Ch 7 — Memory Is the First Constraint
evidence: Fig 7.7 in-figure text: 'Concurrency budget — one 8×H100 host / 140 GB weights / ~64 GB runtime/NCCL / ~436 GB KV budget / 640 GB pool / in-flight ≈ KV budget ÷ KV per request / ≈ 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB ≈ 17.5 → ~17 requests'. Caption: "Naming note: the arithmetic panel reads 'in-flight'; that quantity is the KV-resident slot count (concurrent sequences holding a KV slot), not the Little's-Law in-flight request count."
issue: Figure-vs-caption contradiction, same defect family as FR-001/XR-005 but a distinct artifact. The caption concedes that the figure's own label is the wrong term and issues a naming note instead of correcting the figure. Since the book uses 'in-flight' throughout for the Little's-Law quantity (e.g. p. 85: 'the in-flight concurrency λ·W ≈ 344'; p. 100: '344 in flight'), leaving 'in-flight' inside a figure that means something else — and doing so with an in-caption erratum — is an active trap for a reader who consults figures rather than captions. The List of Figures entry (p. 10) reads 'The concurrency budget' with no indication that the figure's headline label uses a term the book elsewhere reserves for a different quantity.
fix_instruction: Relabel the Fig 7.7 panel to 'KV-resident slots ≈ KV budget ÷ KV per request' and delete the caption's naming note (or reduce it to a one-line pointer). Add 'KV-resident slots' as the term used in all body references so the figure, caption, §7.3, §4.6 and Ch 17 agree.

chapter: Ch 7 — Memory Is the First Constraint
evidence: Fig 7.8 in-figure labels: 'Memory Tetris: how the 8×H100 host (640 GB) fills with context', 'KV cache (grows with context)', 'weights 140 GB', 'runtime / NCCL ~64 GB', 'KV 24.9 GB', '9.5K context = 229 GB used', 'KV 84 GB', '32K context = 288 GB used', 'KV 335 GB', '128K context = 539 GB used', '640 GB = 8× 80 GB ranks (light rules = 80 GB rank boundaries)'. Caption: "The totals are 228.9 GB at 9.5K (shown as 229), 287.9 GB at 32K (shown as 288) and 539.5 GB at 128K (the figure’s scale label reads 539); that 0.5 GB is a label-rounding artifact against a 640 GB axis, not a capacity claim."
issue: Figure-vs-caption numeric-label divergence left in the artifact and excused in the caption. The figure's scale label reads 539 GB while the underlying total is 539.5 GB; the caption explains this away but the figure is the artifact a reader consults. The same figure also labels the 32K KV block as 'KV 84 GB' while the book's own body figure for 32K is 83.9 GB (Table 7-1, p. 126: '32K input KV cache … 83.9 GB'; and Fig 7.5's caption on p. 147: 'at 128K the FP16 KV footprint is ~335 GB'), and the 128K block as 'KV 335 GB' where Table 7-1 says 335.5 GB. Two different rounding conventions ('84' vs '83.9', '335' vs '335.5', '539' vs '539.5') coexist inside one figure with the caption calling out only the last. Per the recurrence rule this rounding-drift family also appears on p. 146 ('KV cache per token (FP16) … ≈ 2.62 MB' with the exact 2,621,440 B given elsewhere) and on p. 147's '83.9 GB'/'335.5 GB' versus Fig 7.5's axis text.
fix_instruction: Adopt one rounding rule for the whole chapter (the chapter states it on p. 145: 'per-request KV is quoted as 24.9 GB (byte-accurate 24.90368 GB)'), apply it to every in-figure label (84 → 83.9, 335 → 335.5, 539 → 539.5), and remove the caption's rounding-apology paragraph. Then reconcile Table 7-1, Fig 7.5's axis text and Fig 7.8 to the same rule.

evidence: Figure 2 (p. 15-16 of PDF) in-figure labels: 'token → cost? Ch4', 'fits host? → KV Ch3/7', 'which phase binds? Ch2/8', '1 host or fleet? Ch17', 'who serves it? Ch10/11/20', 'is it the right call? Ch16/22/25'. Caption: "B (right): question-by-question: six independent navigation prompts, each mapped to the chapter that answers it. These question-to-chapter links are starting points, not complete coverage: one question often spans several chapters, and the decision-justification chapters (Ch. 22 for the design loop, Ch. 25 for the recorded Architecture Decision Record) carry the reasoning the prompt points toward."
issue: Figure-vs-caption and List-of-Figures inconsistency in the figure's own reference syntax. The figure's in-figure pointers use a bare chapter-number form ('Ch4', 'Ch3/7', 'Ch2/8', 'Ch16/22/25') with no § anchors and with inconsistent spacing ('Ch4' vs 'Ch 3/7'), whereas the caption refers to 'Ch. 22' and 'Ch. 25' — the same targets in two different notations. More substantively, the mapping in the figure does not match the Preface's own checklist (p. 14): the figure maps 'fits host? → KV' to 'Ch3/7' and 'which phase binds?' to 'Ch2/8', matching the checklist's Q2/Q3 — but the figure's first prompt, 'token → cost?', is mapped only to 'Ch4', whereas the checklist's Q1 is 'What is the workload?' (Ch 4) and token accounting is spread across Chs 1–3; 'token → cost?' therefore has no chapter that answers it as posed. The caption's claim that each prompt is 'mapped to the chapter that answers it' is thus not true for the first prompt.

chapter: Ch 7 — Memory Is the First Constraint
evidence: p. 144 (Ch 7 §7.1): "The residency floor has two distinct regimes. For inference, the floor is weights + KV: … inference ~164.1 GB for a 70B model at FP16 with 9.2K input (140 + 24.1; the 9.5K-max is 164.9 ≈ 165 GB) … fine-tuning exceeding 1 TB". p. 146 (Table 7-1): "inference residency (weights + KV, 9.5K max) ≈ 165 GB — 140 + 24.9 GB"; 'fits 8×H100 at 9.2K? yes — 164.1 GB < 640 GB'. p. 148 (Fig 7.6 in-figure): '~165 GB'. p. 163 (Ch 7 §7.6): "the max end-of-generation residency ≈ 165 GB". p. 28 (Ch 1 §1.1.5): "At 9.2K tokens the canonical FP16 KV per request is ~24.1 GB … 9,200 × 2,621,440 B = 24,117,248,000 B ≈ 24.12 GB". p. 163: "FP8 KV ≈ 50% of FP16 … dropping the 9.5K max residency from ~165 GB toward ~152 GB". p. 155 (Table 7-2): "inference with FP8 KV … ~152 GB (9.5K; 140 + 12.45; KV alone 12.45 GB)".
issue: Definitional drift in the KV-per-request basis, and a decimal/rounding inconsistency in the same quantity across chapters. Ch 1 states the canonical 9.2K KV as '~24.1 GB' with the exact figure '≈ 24.12 GB'; Ch 7 Table 7-1 states '9,200 ×2.62 MB ≈ 24.1 GB' and the 9.5K basis as '≈ 24.9 GB' (exact 24.90368 GB, stated in the p. 145 rounding rule). Ch 3 Table 3-3 uses '~24.1 GB' at 9.2K and '~12.06 GB' at 8-bit. Ch 5 Table 5-2 uses '~24.1 GB (FP16 KV cache, initial)'. So 24.1 GB (Ch 1's 24.12) and 24.9 GB (Ch 7's 24.90) are both live 'canonical' values for the same quantity at the same context, differing by the input-only vs input+output basis — which Ch 4 Table 4-2 does document ('~24.1 GB @ 9.2K input-only; ~24.9 GB @ 9.5K input+output — the resident slot-counting basis, §4.6'), so the basis is defined once but the Ch 1 and Ch 5 usages do not carry it. Separately, the FP8 9.5K KV figure is '12.06 GB' in Chs 1 and 3 (at the 9.2K input basis) but '12.45 GB' in Ch 7 Table 7-2 and §7.6 (at the 9.5K resident basis) — and p. 28 (Ch 1) explicitly warns against the FP8 figure being quoted at the wrong basis ('the 8-bit variant is not ~13.4 GB'), which shows the book knows the basis matters. A reader comparing '~12.06 GB' (Ch 1/3) with '~12.45 GB' (Ch 7) sees an unexplained 3% discrepancy for the same named quantity ('FP8 KV for the canonical request').
fix_instruction: State the basis inside every quoted KV-per-request figure (e.g. '24.1 GB @ 9.2K input-only' / '24.9 GB @ 9.5K resident'), and reconcile the FP8 pair explicitly: add a line to Table 7-1 giving the FP8 9.2K figure as 12.06 GB alongside the 9.5K figure as 12.45 GB, so Chs 1, 3, 5 and 7 all quote both bases for both precisions. Apply the same to the residency totals: '164.1 GB @ 9.2K' vs '165 GB @ 9.5K' should always carry the basis.

chapter: Ch 7 — Memory Is the First Constraint
evidence: p. 145 (Ch 7 §7.3): "Rounding rule for this section: per-request KV is quoted as 24.9 GB (byte-accurate 24.90368 GB); every quotient below is computed on the byte-accurate value and then floored to whole slots, and the FP8 figure of 12.45 GB is the raw byte-halving of that same value (12.45184 GB)." Compare p. 143 (Ch 7 §7.1): "the ~64 GB is a planning reserve, not a measured constant." Compare p. 149 (Fig 7.7 caption): '436 GB KV budget'; p. 168 (Fig 7.5 caption): 'the ~436 GB KV budget = 640 GB aggregate pool − 140 GB weights − 64 GB runtime/workspace'.
issue: Rounding-rule scope conflict and an undeclared denominator for the KV budget. Ch 7 §7.3 declares a section-scoped rounding rule ('per-request KV is quoted as 24.9 GB … every quotient below is computed on the byte-accurate value'), but the same chapter's §7.1 (p. 143) and §7.2–7.3 elsewhere quote 24.1 GB at 9.2K, and Chs 1, 3 and 5 quote the same quantity as '~24.1 GB' with the exact byte count given as 24,117,248,000 B ≈ 24.12 GB — a third value for the same quantity. Separately, the '436 GB KV budget' is used as the denominator for the concurrency screen (436 ÷ 24.90368 = 17.51 → 17) but is itself a rounded figure: 640 − 140 − 64 = 436 exactly, so the budget is exact while the per-request value is not, and the chapter's §7.1 explicitly makes the 64 GB reserve an [ASSUMPTION] that 'must come from a deployment benchmark' — meaning the 17-slot ceiling inherits an unmeasured denominator without a sensitivity note. By contrast p. 143's unit-basis note says the vendor-binary reading would give '~480 GB' and '~19' slots, so the book knows the denominator is convention-dependent but the canonical figures do not carry the caveat into the tables that consume them.
fix_instruction: Promote the rounding rule from §7.3 to the chapter intro (or the Preface's conventions) and apply it book-wide; state the KV budget as '436 GB (640 − 140 − 64, where the 64 GB runtime reserve is an [ASSUMPTION])' in every table/figure that consumes it, and add a one-line sensitivity (vendor-binary basis: 480 GB → 19 slots) to Table 7-1 or Fig 7.7 so the denominator's convention-dependence travels with the number.

chapter: Ch 4 — The Anatomy of an AI Workload
evidence: p. 110 (Ch 4 §4.8): "Using the canonical per-host bound from § 7.3 and Ch 20 (a single 8×H100 host serves ~2.0 rps at full modeled utilization, i.e. the whole-slot floor 17 KV-resident requests ÷ 8.6 s = 1.977 …)" — compare p. 100 (Ch 4 §4.3): "a single 8×H100 host holds ~17.5 KV-resident requests (436 GB KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per 9.5K-token resident request ≈ 17.51, §4.6)" and p. 113 (Ch 4 §4.8) also citing '§ 7.3' for the per-host bound.
issue: Cross-chapter definitional drift in the canonical 'model baseline' and in the per-host capacity bound, and a bare section pointer whose target does not carry the cited quantity. The per-host bound '~2.0 rps' is attributed to '§ 7.3 and Ch 20', but §7.3 (p. 145-150) is the memory/KV-arithmetic section: it derives the 17-slot concurrency ceiling and the ~436 GB KV budget but never computes an rps per host (17 ÷ 8.6 s = 1.977 rps is first computed here, in Ch 4 §4.8, and later used in Ch 17/20). So the pointer attributes to § 7.3 a quantity § 7.3 does not contain — the 'target actually discusses the cited topic' check fails. Second, the canonical 'model baseline' is defined differently in different places: Table 4-2 (p. 64) says 'Model baseline: Dense 70B' with 'Attention architecture: full-MHA reference model (K/V width = hidden_dim)'; Ch 7 (p. 145) calls it 'a canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA 70B reference model'; Ch 5 (p. 98) calls it 'the canonical full-MHA 70B reference (80 layers, hidden 8192, no GQA — the constructed teaching geometry of Ch 4 Table 4-2)'; but Ch 4 Table 4-2 also names 'Model parameters: 70B [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] reference model' while Ch 3 Table 3-1 labels the same object 'Total parameters 70B [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] reference model' and Ch 3 §3.3.1 says 'The 70B dense full-MHA model below is a constructed teaching reference (the canonical scenario, Ch 4 Table 4-2)'. The term 'model baseline' itself appears only in Table 4-2 and nowhere else, so a reader seeking the canonical model definition has no single authority and must assemble it from Chs 3, 4, 5 and 7.
fix_instruction: Either move the 17 ÷ 8.6 s = 1.977 rps derivation into §7.3 (where the 17-slot ceiling is derived) and keep the Ch 4 §4.8 pointer, or re-point the §4.8 citation to Ch 17 (Table 17-1) / Ch 20, where the per-host rps bound is actually tabulated. Separately, define the canonical model once — in the Ch 4 Canonical Workload box (Table 4-2) — with the phrase 'canonical 70B full-MHA teaching model (80 layers, hidden 8192, 64 query heads, head dim 128, FP16 weights, FP16 KV)', and make Chs 3, 5 and 7 cite that definition by name rather than restating partial variants of it.

evidence: "The two-point approximation of the mean is E[L] ≈0.99 × 0.8 + 0.01 × 5.0 ≈0.84 s — looks fine. Three related numbers circulate in this paragraph, so we fix them once here, at first presentation: the two-point analytic mean is 0.842 s (0.99 × 0.8 + 0.01 × 5.0, written 0.84 s above); the plotted synthetic stream’s exact mean is 0.85 s (the value Fig 6.2 displays); and every percentile below is a property of the N = 10,000 sample, not of the distribution — the population p99 of this 99 % log-normal + 1 % straggler mixture is 5.0 s. Read off the sample, the long tail looks like this: p50 ≈ 0.80 s, p90 ≈ 0.94 s, p95 ≈ 0.99 s, and p99 ≈ 1.33 s — a knife-edge property of this N = 10,000 sample, not of the distribution: linear interpolation lands just past the largest non-straggler draw, between it and the first straggler (percentile position 1 + (N−1)×0.99 = 9,900.01; sorted-sample ranks: 9,900 → 1.30 s, 9,901 → 5.0 s; 1.30 + 0.01 × (5.0 − 1.30) ≈ 1.33 s), and the sample figure is knife-edge in the straggler count as well: with exactly 100 stragglers (1 % of 10,000) the interpolation above returns 1.33 s, while 101 of 10,000 puts a straggler at rank 9,900 itself, so both interpolation endpoints are 5.0 s draws and the sample p99 is 5.0 s."
issue: ASD-STE100 readability defect: one sentence carries seven distinct qualifications, an interpolation formula, two rank positions and a conditional-counterfactual, and the paragraph re-states the same mean three times (0.84 / 0.842 / 0.85) with the parenthetical 'written 0.84 s above' pointing at a sentence the reader has just read. The 'knife-edge' reasoning (linear interpolation between rank 9,900 and 9,901) is a reproducibility note, not a body-text argument, and it is interleaved with the percentile claims it qualifies. The same sentence-level pattern recurs at p. 139 ('Three related numbers circulate…'), p. 111 and p. 145 — a recurring house style of embedding multi-clause reconciliation inside a single sentence. A reader chasing the headline (p99 ≈ 1.33 s vs population 5.0 s) must parse the whole apparatus before learning the point.
fix_instruction: Split the paragraph: (1) state the four sample percentiles as a list; (2) state in one sentence that the sample p99 is knife-edge and why (one straggler changes it from 1.33 s to 5.0 s); (3) move the interpolation arithmetic (percentile position, rank values, the 1.30 + 0.01 × (5.0 − 1.30) computation) into a reproducibility note below the paragraph, consistent with the note style already used in the Fig 6.2 caption on p. 133. Remove the redundant restatement of 0.842 s.

evidence: "Every load-bearing quantitative claim carries Axes 1 and 2 as an inline pair (e.g. [1P][DERIVED]); Axis 3, measurement status, rides along where a claim’s status is known. A claim carries the labels directly (inline) or via an identified table or section that states them (e.g. a worked-example table whose header or footnote gives provenance and status for every row); purely illustrative or rhetorical numbers that no later calculation depends on may carry them in the surrounding prose — exceptions are defined unambiguously in the Sources, Method, and Reproducibility chapter."
issue: Two-claims-in-one-rule defect with an internal contradiction. The rule says every load-bearing quantitative claim carries the pair inline, then immediately allows 'via an identified table or section that states them', then allows 'purely illustrative or rhetorical numbers' to carry labels only in surrounding prose — and defers the exception definitions to a chapter the reader has not yet reached. The contradiction is that a claim 'via an identified table' cannot carry an inline pair, yet the same paragraph asserts that every load-bearing claim 'carries Axes 1 and 2 as an inline pair'. This is the rule that the body then implements inconsistently (e.g. p. 90 Table 4-2 carries per-row Axis-1/Axis-2 tags — compliant — but p. 102's cost-basis table and p. 116's Table 5-2 mix tagged and untagged rows, and p. 131's Fig 6.2 note leaves the synthetic stream's construction untagged in the caption). The rule's own escape clause ('exceptions are defined unambiguously in the Sources, Method, and Reproducibility chapter') means the operative definition of the label system is not in the Preface where the system is introduced.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the rule as three explicit, non-overlapping sentences: (1) every load-bearing quantity carries an Axis-1 and Axis-2 tag, inline or in the caption/footnote of the identified table or figure that contains it; (2) the Axis-3 status is optional but must appear when the status is known; (3) rhetorical numbers that no calculation depends on may be untagged. Move the exception definitions into the Preface itself and delete the deferral to the later chapter, or state that the later chapter's definitions override the Preface's.
